CURRENT EU STATUS: EU providers hold ~15% of EU cloud market; US hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, GCP) hold ~70%
KEY VULNERABILITY: Structural lock-in to non-EU platforms; US providers invest ~EUR 10bn/quarter in EU capex, outpacing local competition
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Demand Accelerators for EU-designed chips used in cloud infrastructure; innovation procurement mandating EU-designed silicon in public cloud
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: Cloud Sovereignty Framework with 4 SEAL levels; mandatory sovereignty risk assessments for public-sector procurement; tripling EU data centre capacity by 2035
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 200bn for cloud/AI data centres (mostly private)
KEY EU PLAYERS: OVHcloud, Scaleway, STACKIT, Deutsche Telekom/T-Systems, SAP, Post Telecom
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU loses ability to control data residency and processing; extraterritorial legal exposure under US CLOUD Act and FISA 702
REFERENCE / SOURCE: Synergy Research Group 2025; COM(2026) 503 final

CURRENT EU STATUS: 80%+ of EU digital products/services/infrastructure relies on non-EU providers; EU awarded EUR 180m sovereign cloud tender (Apr 2026)
KEY VULNERABILITY: Extraterritorial data access risk under non-EU jurisdiction; limited EU control over cloud software stacks, APIs, and operational management
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Strategic Projects designation for semiconductor facilities serving sovereign cloud use cases; B2B Supply Chain Platform for chip supply visibility
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: 4-tier sovereignty assurance (SEAL-1 to SEAL-4); SEAL-4 requires exclusive EU control, EU-only data processing, open APIs; obligation for public-sector sovereignty risk assessments
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Included in EUR 200bn cloud/AI investment envelope
KEY EU PLAYERS: Proximus/S3NS (Thales-Google JV), CleverCloud, Clarence, Mistral AI
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: US hyperscaler software stacks, VMware (Broadcom), Kubernetes ecosystem
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Public-sector data exposed to foreign intelligence access; inability to ensure digital sovereignty for critical government functions
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EC sovereign cloud tender IP/26/833; Cloud Sovereignty Framework document

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU cloud providers rely almost entirely on non-EU server hardware (Intel/AMD CPUs, NVIDIA GPUs); no EU-based leading-edge logic foundry
KEY VULNERABILITY: Complete dependency on US-designed processors and Asian fabrication; server motherboard/PCB supply concentrated in Asia
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: First-of-a-Kind facility support extended to PCBs, packaging, and assembly; EU open foundry for 3nm-and-below manufacturing (pilot 2030-2033); Chips Fund for semiconductor startups
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA strategic data centre projects must demonstrate innovation and sustainability; R&D funding of ~EUR 2bn over 7 years for next-gen cloud/AI technologies
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 120bn total semiconductor investment (EUR 30bn for advanced foundry)
KEY EU PLAYERS: ASML (lithography), NXP, Infineon, STMicroelectronics, ARM (UK-based, chip design)
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: TSMC (fabrication), Samsung (fabrication), Intel (design+fab), NVIDIA (GPU design), AMD (CPU/GPU design)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU cloud infrastructure permanently dependent on foreign chip designers and fabricators; supply disruption risk from geopolitical tensions (Taiwan Strait)
REFERENCE / SOURCE: COM(2026) 503 final; EE Times analysis June 2026

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU FLAP-D colocation at 3.6 GW (doubled since 2019); vacancy compressing to 6.5% by end-2026; Ireland data centres consume 22% of national metered electricity
KEY VULNERABILITY: Insufficient capacity for AI workload growth; energy constraints are now the binding bottleneck (not chips or capital); uneven geographic distribution across member states
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Demand Accelerators linking chip production to data centre build-out; synergies with AI Factories and Gigafactories as anchor demand for EU-made chips
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA aims to triple EU data centre capacity in 5-7 years (by 2031-2033); streamlined permitting framework; strategic project designation for innovative/sustainable facilities
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 200bn for cloud/AI data centres
KEY EU PLAYERS: Equinix, Digital Realty (US-headquartered but EU-operating), European colocation operators, national telecoms
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: US hyperscalers drive most new builds; US-designed chips power virtually all AI racks
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU unable to meet exploding AI compute demand; AI development migrates to US/Asia; competitive disadvantage for EU enterprises and researchers
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EU AI Infrastructure Report 2026 (alicelabs.ai); CBRE forecasts; CSO Ireland data

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU has no domestic high-performance AI GPU at scale; NVIDIA holds >80% AI accelerator market; EU AI chip startups (e.g. Axelera, SiPearl, Tenstorrent EU) are pre-scale
KEY VULNERABILITY: Total dependency on NVIDIA/AMD for AI training and inference accelerators; US export controls can restrict access; EU AI chip startups lack volume manufacturing access
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Grand Challenges for AI chip development; public innovation procurement to validate EU AI silicon in data centre racks; preferential treatment of domestic AI silicon in sovereign cloud/defence procurement
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA AI Gigafactory programme (min. 75,000 advanced AI accelerators per facility); R&D funding for full-stack AI solutions with competitive performance-per-watt
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of EUR 120bn semiconductor envelope + EUR 200bn data centre envelope
TIMELINE: AI Gigafactory call expected Jul 2026; foundry 2030-2033
KEY EU PLAYERS: Axelera AI (Netherlands), SiPearl (France), Graphcore (UK), Tenstorrent (EU operations)
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: NVIDIA (H100/B200/GB200), AMD (MI300/MI400), Google (TPU), Broadcom (custom ASICs)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU AI sovereignty structurally impossible without domestic accelerator production; geopolitical leverage point for US/Asia
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EE Times June 2026; COM(2026) 503 final; Akin Gump analysis

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU produces <10% of global semiconductors; virtually no EU-designed leading-edge AI chips; design tools (EDA) dominated by US firms (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA)
KEY VULNERABILITY: Dependency on US EDA software for all chip design; lack of EU-based fabless AI chip companies at scale; advanced node PDKs controlled by non-EU foundries
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips for Europe Initiative 2.0: cloud-based design platform for EU designers; pilot line industrialisation; competence centres; Chips Fund for startups/scaleups/SMEs
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA supports open-source AI model development and deployment, creating downstream demand for EU-designed inference chips
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of Chips for Europe Initiative budget
TIMELINE: Design platform operational progressively; Chips Fund ongoing
KEY EU PLAYERS: Imec (Belgium, R&D), Fraunhofer (Germany, R&D), CEA-Leti (France, R&D), European EDA startups
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA (US/German), ARM (UK/Japan), TSMC/Samsung (PDKs and process nodes)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU permanently relegated to chip consumer rather than designer; innovation captured outside EU; brain drain of semiconductor talent
REFERENCE / SOURCE: COM(2026) 503 final; Chips for Europe Initiative documentation

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU lacks production-scale advanced packaging (chiplet integration, 3D stacking, heterogeneous integration); identified as most significant near-term structural gap for AI
KEY VULNERABILITY: Chiplet/3D packaging essential for modern AI chips; capacity concentrated in TSMC (CoWoS), ASE, Amkor (Asia); EU has no equivalent facility
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: First-of-a-Kind support explicitly expanded to advanced packaging and assembly; EU foundry will combine leading-edge nodes with chiplet integration and 3D packaging
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA strategic projects may include packaging facilities co-located with data centres
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of EUR 30bn advanced foundry allocation
KEY EU PLAYERS: Imec (packaging R&D), ASML, various EU OSAT concepts
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: TSMC CoWoS, ASE Group, Amkor Technology (all Asia-based)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: AI chip performance constrained by packaging bottleneck; EU foundry output unusable for modern AI workloads without domestic packaging
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EE Times June 2026; COM(2026) 503 final

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU has 14 EuroHPC supercomputers + 19 AI Factories; access mechanisms include Playground (2 working days) and Fast Lane (50,000 GPU-hours); but scale insufficient vs. US frontier labs
KEY VULNERABILITY: Frontier LLM training requires 10,000-100,000+ GPU clusters; EU lacks such concentrated compute; EU AI labs (Mistral, Aleph Alpha) train on US cloud infrastructure
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips Act 2.0 Demand Accelerators create procurement pathways for EU chips in AI training clusters; Grand Challenges target AI chip industrial development
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA AI Gigafactories (each with min. 75,000 accelerators) designed specifically for frontier AI training; R&D support for next-gen cloud and AI technologies
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Covered by CADA + semiconductor investment envelopes
TIMELINE: AI Gigafactory call Jul 2026; operational target 2028-2030
KEY EU PLAYERS: Mistral AI (France), Aleph Alpha (Germany), EuroHPC JU, national HPC centres
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: NVIDIA (GPUs), US cloud providers (training infrastructure), OpenAI/Anthropic/Google (model competition)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU unable to train competitive frontier models domestically; dependent on US providers for foundational AI capabilities; strategic vulnerability in AI race
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EU AI Infrastructure Report 2026; AI Continent Action Plan

CURRENT EU STATUS: LLM inference increasingly moves to edge and lower-power chips; EU has emerging strengths in low-power/embedded processors (ARM-based, RISC-V) but no scaled inference accelerator
KEY VULNERABILITY: Growing demand for efficient inference silicon as LLM deployment scales; EU lacks domestic inference-optimised accelerators; inference workloads represent growing share of AI chip market
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Public innovation procurement allows public administrations to buy data centre racks with EU AI chips for inference validation; Demand Accelerators create market pull for EU inference silicon
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA sovereignty framework incentivises EU-controlled AI inference (SEAL levels assess AI inference data processing location and control); open-source-first principle for public-sector AI software
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of broader semiconductor and AI investment envelopes
KEY EU PLAYERS: Axelera AI (inference accelerators), SiPearl (HPC processors), RISC-V ecosystem in EU
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: NVIDIA (inference GPUs), AMD, Qualcomm (edge inference), Google (TPU inference), AWS (Inferentia/Trainium)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU LLM deployment permanently reliant on foreign inference hardware; sovereignty framework undermined if inference runs on non-EU controlled silicon
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EE Times June 2026; CADA sovereignty framework; Euronews draft analysis

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU has Mistral AI as leading open-weight model provider; most enterprise LLM deployment uses US models (OpenAI/GPT, Anthropic/Claude, Google/Gemini, Meta/Llama) on US infrastructure
KEY VULNERABILITY: EU model ecosystem growing but far behind US in scale/investment; model training data governance unclear; fine-tuning and deployment typically on US cloud platforms
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips Act 2.0 indirectly supports by creating domestic hardware substrate for model training/inference; linkage to EU Open Source Strategy
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA open-source-first principle for public-sector AI procurement; sovereignty risk assessments must evaluate AI model control and data pipeline governance; SEAL levels assess AI model hosting jurisdiction
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 2bn R&D for cloud/AI technologies under CADA
KEY EU PLAYERS: Mistral AI, Aleph Alpha, various EU AI research labs (LAION, BLOOM legacy), Hugging Face (France/US)
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, xAI
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU enterprises and governments depend on US-controlled AI models with opaque training data and governance; strategic dependency on US AI ecosystem
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EU Open Source Strategy; CADA proposal; COM(2026) 503 final

CURRENT EU STATUS: HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) essential for LLM training/inference; market dominated by SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron; EU has no HBM production; advanced interconnects (NVLink, InfiniBand) US-controlled
KEY VULNERABILITY: HBM supply constrained globally; EU entirely dependent on Korean/US memory manufacturers; networking fabric (InfiniBand/NVIDIA, Ethernet switches) also US/Asia-sourced
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Strategic Projects can cover memory and interconnect facilities; B2B Supply Chain Platform improves visibility into memory supply risks; risk assessment guidance for exposed sectors
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA strategic project designation may extend to facilities supporting AI infrastructure supply chain
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of EUR 120bn semiconductor investment
KEY EU PLAYERS: EU memory R&D limited; some DRAM design capability in legacy European firms; interconnect R&D at research institutes
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron (HBM); NVIDIA (NVLink, InfiniBand via Mellanox); Broadcom (networking ASICs)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Bottleneck for any EU AI infrastructure build-out; AI Gigafactories depend on non-EU memory and interconnect supply
REFERENCE / SOURCE: COM(2026) 503 final; semiconductor industry analysis

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU operates 6 quantum pilot lines (superconducting, photonic, neutral atom, semiconducting/quantum dot, diamond-based, trapped ion); EUR 50m funding each; Chips JU coordinates
KEY VULNERABILITY: Strong R&D base but limited path to industrial-scale quantum chip production; different qubit modalities require different fabrication processes; gap between lab and fab
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips for Europe Initiative 2.0 supports quantum chip design libraries, pilot line industrialisation, cleanrooms, foundries for prototyping; EUR 20m call for quantum-enabling technologies (Jul-Sep 2026)
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA indirectly supports by building data centre infrastructure that can host quantum-classical hybrid systems
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 300m+ for quantum pilot lines (6 x EUR 50m + enabling tech calls)
KEY EU PLAYERS: IQM (Finland, superconducting), Pasqal (France, neutral atom), QuiX Quantum (Netherlands, photonic), Alpine Quantum Technologies (Austria, trapped ion)
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: IBM, Google, Amazon (Braket), IonQ, Quantinuum (US/UK)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU loses first-mover advantage in quantum computing; dependent on US/China quantum platforms for future computation
REFERENCE / SOURCE: Chips JU quantum pilot lines; QuIC Position Paper; PRADEEP's TECHPOINTS

CURRENT EU STATUS: PIXEurope pilot line supports photonic integrated circuits (PICs) but focused on telecom near-infrared wavelengths; quantum modalities (ion-trap, neutral-atom) need visible/UV range (295-800nm) not yet supported
KEY VULNERABILITY: Photonic chips for quantum computing require non-standard wavelengths and materials incompatible with CMOS; fabrication limited to bespoke academic cleanrooms; not scalable to industrial reliability
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips Act 2.0 reinforces photonics and photonic integrated circuits as priority area; pilot line support extended; industrialisation of existing quantum pilot lines
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: Not directly addressed by CADA
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of Chips for Europe Initiative and quantum pilot line budgets
TIMELINE: Progressive; aligned with broader pilot line timelines
KEY EU PLAYERS: PIXEurope consortium, LioniX International (Netherlands), SMART Photonics (Netherlands), III-V Lab (France)
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: US photonic chip companies; Asian foundries with broader wavelength capabilities
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Quantum computing platforms (ion-trap
REFERENCE / SOURCE: neutral-atom) cannot scale commercially in EU without appropriate photonic chip supply; EU quantum advantage eroded
column14: QuIC Position Paper Dec 2025; PIXEurope pilot line documentation

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU has R&D in cryogenic control electronics, readout systems, and quantum interconnects; Chips JU call specifically targets enabling technologies (not QPUs themselves)
KEY VULNERABILITY: Quantum processors require specialised control electronics operating at millikelvin temperatures; cryogenic CMOS, photonic interconnects, and packaging for modular quantum systems are nascent globally
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips JU EUR 20m call for quantum-enabling technologies (Jul-Sep 2026); scope includes cryogenic electronics, photonic components, transduction, packaging for modular assemblies; must interface with EU foundries/pilot lines
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: Not directly addressed by CADA
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 20m (EUR 5-7m per project); 36-48 month project duration
KEY EU PLAYERS: European quantum hardware startups, university spin-offs, Chips JU participants (EU/EEA + select partners: Canada, Israel, Korea, NZ, Switzerland, UK)
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: US quantum hardware companies with integrated control stacks; dilution refrigerator suppliers (Bluefors is Finnish - EU strength)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Without scaled enabling electronics quantum chips remain lab curiosities; system-level integration gap prevents commercialisation
REFERENCE / SOURCE: Chips JU quantum-enabling call Feb 2026 presentation

CURRENT EU STATUS: EuroHPC operates 10 quantum systems alongside supercomputers; hybrid quantum-classical computing emerging as practical paradigm; cloud access to quantum via US platforms (IBM, Amazon Braket, Azure Quantum)
KEY VULNERABILITY: EU quantum hardware exists but cloud-accessible quantum computing dominated by US platforms; integration of quantum accelerators into classical HPC/AI workflows requires middleware and orchestration software
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips Act 2.0 Strategic Projects can support quantum-classical integration facilities; Demand Accelerators may extend to quantum-enhanced computing use cases
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA data centre framework could accommodate quantum-ready facilities; R&D funding for next-gen computing technologies
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of EuroHPC and CADA R&D budgets
KEY EU PLAYERS: EuroHPC JU, Atos/Eviden (France, quantum integration), IQM, Pasqal, European quantum software companies
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: IBM Quantum, Amazon Braket, Microsoft Azure Quantum, Google Quantum AI
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU researchers and enterprises access quantum computing through US cloud platforms; strategic dependency mirrors classical cloud dependency pattern
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EuroHPC programme documentation; EU AI Infrastructure Report 2026

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) requires new hardware security modules and crypto-accelerator chips; EU has strength in security chips (NXP, Infineon) but PQC-specific silicon is early-stage
KEY VULNERABILITY: Quantum computers threaten current encryption; hardware must be upgraded with PQC algorithms; timeline pressure as quantum capability advances; EU has strong position in secure element chips
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips Act 2.0 supports mainstream chip innovation including security applications; First-of-a-Kind provisions cover security-relevant semiconductor innovation; EU strength in automotive/industrial/security chips reinforced
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA sovereignty framework SEAL levels include cybersecurity requirements that will increasingly need PQC compliance
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of broader semiconductor investment
TIMELINE: Progressive; PQC standardisation ongoing (NIST standards published 2024)
KEY EU PLAYERS: NXP Semiconductors (Netherlands), Infineon (Germany), STMicroelectronics (France/Italy), EU cryptography research community
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: NIST PQC standards (US-led but open); US chipmakers integrating PQC; potential advantage for EU security chip leaders
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: EU enterprises and governments vulnerable to harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks if PQC hardware transition delayed
REFERENCE / SOURCE: NIST PQC standardisation; EU cybersecurity strategy

CURRENT EU STATUS: ASML (Netherlands) holds global monopoly on EUV lithography; EU also strong in specialty equipment; but some critical tool segments (etch, deposition, inspection) are US/Japan-dominated
KEY VULNERABILITY: ASML is indispensable global chokepoint; but EU depends on US/Japan for complementary equipment (Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, KLA); export control alignment with US is geopolitically sensitive
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips Act 2.0 reinforces EU equipment ecosystem; Strategic Projects can include equipment manufacturing; fast-track permitting; Semiconductor Regions of Excellence label
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: Not directly addressed by CADA
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of EUR 120bn semiconductor investment
KEY EU PLAYERS: ASML (Netherlands), Zeiss (Germany, EUV optics), BESI (Netherlands, packaging equipment), various EU equipment SMEs
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: Applied Materials (US), Lam Research (US), Tokyo Electron (Japan), KLA (US), Screen Holdings (Japan)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Loss of EU equipment leadership would eliminate key leverage point in global semiconductor value chain; ASML export restrictions are geopolitical flashpoint
REFERENCE / SOURCE: COM(2026) 503 final; global semiconductor equipment market analysis

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU has strengths in specialty materials (Siltronic, SOITEC) and rare earth processing capacity; but critical raw materials (gallium, germanium, rare earths) concentrated in China
KEY VULNERABILITY: China controls ~80% of gallium and ~60% of germanium production; these are essential for compound semiconductors (GaN, SiC) used in power electronics, 5G, and photonics; EU Critical Raw Materials Act provides framework
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Strategic Projects expanded to cover specialty materials across value chain; risk assessment and mitigation guidance for exposed sectors; B2B Supply Chain Platform for supply visibility
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: Not directly addressed by CADA
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Part of EUR 120bn semiconductor investment; synergies with EU Critical Raw Materials Act
TIMELINE: Ongoing; aligned with Critical Raw Materials Act implementation
KEY EU PLAYERS: Siltronic (Germany, wafers), SOITEC (France, SOI substrates), Umicore (Belgium, materials), various EU chemical companies
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: China (gallium, germanium, rare earths), Japan (specialty chemicals, photoresists), US (specialty gases)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Supply disruption of critical raw materials can halt EU semiconductor production regardless of foundry investment; China export controls on gallium/germanium (imposed 2023) demonstrated vulnerability
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EU Critical Raw Materials Act; China export controls analysis

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU faces significant semiconductor talent shortage; estimated 30,000-50,000 additional workers needed by 2030; competition from US CHIPS Act and Asian expansion for same talent pool
KEY VULNERABILITY: Insufficient graduates in semiconductor engineering; brain drain to US/Asia; ageing workforce in European fabs; new foundries (TSMC Dresden, Intel Magdeburg) competing for same limited talent
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Chips for Europe Initiative 2.0: competence centres network; skills development across semiconductor ecosystem; Semiconductor Regions of Excellence label to attract talent
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA indirectly supports by creating domestic AI/cloud industry jobs that reduce brain drain pressure
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: Not separately quantified; embedded in programme budgets
TIMELINE: Ongoing; urgently needed before new fabs come online 2027-2030
KEY EU PLAYERS: European universities, Imec academy, Fraunhofer, national semiconductor training programmes
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: US universities, TSMC/Samsung training programmes, Asian semiconductor workforce
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: New EU fabs cannot operate without trained workforce; investment wasted if talent gap not closed; critical enabler for all other dependency-reduction measures
REFERENCE / SOURCE: EC semiconductor skills analysis; industry estimates

CURRENT EU STATUS: Original Chips Act introduced crisis response mechanism; Chips Act 2.0 strengthens with proactive tools; 2025 simulation exercise with member states conducted
DEPENDENCY LEVEL (1-5): Improvement over original, but untested in real crisis
KEY VULNERABILITY: 3 - Moderate
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Semiconductor supply chains are 6-18 month lead time; crisis detection and response must be faster; information-sharing by companies currently insufficient; joint purchasing untested
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: B2B Semiconductor Supply Chain Platform for real-time visibility; structured crisis activation process; joint purchasing mechanism; priority orders from publicly subsidised fabs; EU Blueprint for semiconductor crisis management by Q2 2027
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: CADA includes parallel resilience mechanisms for cloud/AI infrastructure; sovereignty risk assessments
TIMELINE: Operational costs embedded in programme budgets
KEY EU PLAYERS: Blueprint by Q2 2027; platform deployment progressive
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: European Semiconductor Board, national authorities, industry participants
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Global supply chain dependencies remain; crisis response depends on cooperation with non-EU suppliers and governments
REFERENCE / SOURCE: Single-point-of-failure supply chains for advanced chips remain until EU foundry operational (2030+); geopolitical crises (Taiwan) could cause multi-year disruption

CURRENT EU STATUS: EU estimates EUR 320bn total needed (EUR 120bn semiconductors + EUR 200bn cloud/AI); EU budget contribution is fraction; bulk must come from private sector and member state co-investment
KEY VULNERABILITY: EU public funding alone insufficient; private investors prefer established US/Asian ecosystems; member state coordination historically difficult; state aid rules add complexity even with simplification
CHIPS ACT 2.0 MEASURE: Strategic Projects with facilitated public investment access; Chips Fund for startups/scaleups/SMEs; simplified State aid assessment for First-of-a-Kind facilities; Competitiveness Coordination Tool for EU-Member State-industry alignment
COMPLEMENTARY CADA MEASURE: CADA strategic project support; public-sector procurement as demand signal; open-source-first principle to lower barriers
ESTIMATED INVESTMENT: EUR 320bn total (EUR 120bn semi + EUR 200bn cloud/AI + EUR 20bn energy digitalisation)
KEY EU PLAYERS: EIB, national development banks, EU venture capital, industry co-investment
KEY NON-EU DEPENDENCIES: US CHIPS Act ($52bn + private leverage), Asian national semiconductor programmes (Korea, Japan, China all >$50bn)
RISK IF UNADDRESSED: Investment shortfall means EU foundry delayed or downscaled; private sector invests elsewhere; EU targets not met; sovereignty goals remain aspirational
REFERENCE / SOURCE: Agence Europe; COM(2026) 503 final; Impact Assessment
